title: Ambrose Makes the Emperor Do Penance
text:
In 390 a riot broke out in Thessalonica, in Greece, and the crowd killed Butheric, the commander of the local garrison. The emperor Theodosius I, furious, ordered a reprisal. Soldiers trapped the people of the city in the circus and massacred them. Theodoret, a church historian of the next century, puts the dead at seven thousand.

Ambrose, the bishop of Milan where Theodosius was then residing, wrote the emperor a private letter, which survives. He told him that he could not offer the Eucharist in his presence until he had repented, and urged him to do public penance, as King David had done.

Theodoret later dramatized the scene, describing Ambrose meeting the emperor at the church door and barring his way. Whatever the exact form, Theodosius submitted. He laid aside his imperial ornaments and did public penance for some months before he was readmitted to communion around Christmas. Theodoret adds that he also passed a law requiring a delay of thirty days between a sentence of death and its execution, so that anger would not decide such matters.
lesson: No position puts you above answering for harm done in anger. Building a pause between rage and action protects everyone, including yourself.
people: Emperor Theodosius I, Ambrose of Milan
source: Ambrose, Letter 51 to Theodosius; Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, Book 5, chapters 17 and 18
caveat: Theodoret's scene at the church door and his death toll are probably embellished; Ambrose's own letter is the reliable source.
